strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored reliability problem in multi-agent vision-language systems: hallucinations propagated through inter-agent communication.
Proposes an intuitive combination of visual-token relay and attention reallocation, supported by token-, layer-, and turn-level analyses.

Reports unusually broad experiments across eight benchmarks, four MAS topologies, ten model variants/sizes, competing hallucination-mitigation methods, component ablations, and different numbers of agent turns.
The main performance tables show consistent improvements across models and benchmarks, while the turn-count experiment directly targets the claimed snowballing behavior.
The paper is generally well organized, and its figures communicate the motivating phenomenon and proposed architecture clearly.
weaknesses: The MAS evaluation protocol is critically underspecified. The paper does not adequately describe agent roles, prompts, message routing, number of agents, stopping rules, how benchmark questions are decomposed, or precisely how linear, layered, random, and circular systems generate the reported predictions. Consequently, the central experiments are difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The claimed causal explanation is not established. Visual attention decreases while the textual history grows across turns, so the reported trend may arise mechanically from attention dilution and changing sequence length. Controls with matched context lengths, irrelevant textual prefixes, independently corrupted messages, or controlled hallucination injection are missing. Attention correlation alone does not demonstrate that reduced visual attention causes hallucination propagation.

The definition of attention allocation appears incomplete or inconsistent: Equations 5–6 sum attention over queries and target-token subsets without an explicit normalization for sequence length or the number of tokens, despite plots presenting allocation on a 0–1 scale. This is especially problematic because token counts change over turns.

The new HS metric is insufficiently validated. Its judge model, judge prompt, severity rubric, construction of propagation distance, annotation reliability, and correlation with human judgments are not reported. The sigmoid weighting is ad hoc, and all competing methods are evaluated using a metric introduced by the authors without independent validation.

The method is described as lightweight and plug-and-play, yet it adds a learned transformer block, modifies internal attention, and uses a two-stage training pipeline. Training datasets are not specified, and there is no matched-control experiment showing that gains are due to ViF rather than additional training, parameters, or exposure to evaluation-like data.

The mathematical description of attention reallocation is ambiguous. Equations 3–4 do not clearly specify how attention is removed from source entries, and the stated conservation of total attention is not evident from the formulation. Head-wise operation, masking order, renormalization, and handling across architectures are also unclear.

The token-dropping study is heavily confounded: zeroing hidden states is not equivalent to removing information, subset construction and cardinality matching are unclear, and interventions at different depths naturally have different downstream effects. It therefore provides limited evidence that the identified 'unimodal' morphology is uniquely responsible for visual grounding.

Reported results omit repeated-run variation, confidence intervals, significance tests, and robustness to decoding seeds despite generation temperature 1 and stochastic/random MAS components. The remarkably uniform gains across a very large experiment grid cannot be assessed statistically.

Benchmark evaluation details are incomplete, particularly the exact GPT-4 judge versions/prompts and whether all methods receive identical tuning and compute. Efficiency claims are unsupported by latency, memory, token-count, parameter-count, or training-cost measurements.

Reproducibility is currently weak: the manuscript only promises future code release, while crucial training data, prompt templates, topology construction, judge configuration, and several implementation details are absent. There are also metric-direction inconsistencies in the appendix tables, such as POPE and AMBER being marked as lower-is-better despite being treated as higher-is-better elsewhere.

strengths: The paper targets an important and comparatively underexplored reliability problem: visual errors may propagate and amplify through multi-agent communication.
The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple VLM families and sizes, four communication topologies, eight benchmarks, token/layer/turn analyses, component ablations, and hyperparameter studies.
Relaying selected visual features alongside textual messages is intuitive, and the Key-Norm alternative attempts to support architectures whose attention matrices are inaccessible.
The reported improvements are consistent across the presented benchmarks, models, and system structures.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is insufficiently established. As textual context grows across turns, normalized attention to a fixed set of visual tokens can decrease mechanically. The paper provides no context-length-matched, message-shuffled, or other controlled experiment separating this effect from genuine loss of visual grounding. Correlation between reduced attention and errors does not establish that it causes hallucination snowballing.

The token-dropping analysis is not a clean causal test. Subsets differ in their selection criteria and apparent cardinality, hidden states are zeroed rather than tokens being removed, and there are no repeated random trials, uncertainty estimates, or matched controls such as top-attention non-unimodal tokens. Consequently, the claimed special role of unimodal tokens remains uncertain.

Essential MAS details are missing: agent roles, prompts, message formats, number of agents and turns used for each result, topology execution rules, stopping conditions, and whether agents independently receive the original image. Without these details, neither the phenomenon nor the reported comparisons are reproducible.

The method is characterized as lightweight and plug-and-play, but it introduces a transformer block and uses two-stage training in which the projector and large language model are trainable. The manuscript omits the training datasets, objectives, number of steps, data mixture, initialization, checkpoint selection, and per-model training procedure. This is a major reproducibility gap and makes the plug-and-play characterization misleading.

Comparative fairness is unclear. ViF is trained specifically for the task, whereas the five competing methods were designed for single-agent inference and appear to be transplanted without comparable adaptation. Important simple baselines are absent, including retransmitting the original image/features, suppressing or truncating prior text, matching ViF's extra token budget with random or top-attention tokens, and fine-tuning the base model with the same data but without ViF.

The proposed HS metric is not validated. Hallucination propagation distance is not operationally defined, the judge model and judging prompt are unspecified, and no agreement with human annotations or sensitivity analysis is reported. Results on this bespoke metric therefore cannot substantiate the claimed 30–40% reduction in snowballing.

The evaluation reports single point estimates despite generation temperature 1 and the use of stochastic or model-judged benchmarks. There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, or judge-variance analyses, so the reliability of modest gains is unknown.

Efficiency claims are unsupported: there are no latency, memory, token-count, communication-bandwidth, or training-cost measurements. Cross-agent transfer of internal visual tokens is also not explained for heterogeneous agents or models with different embedding spaces.

Several technical definitions remain ambiguous, including normalization of attention allocation, exact shallow/middle/deep layer boundaries, construction and training of contextualized relay tokens, and the implementation of attention collection/reallocation. These omissions make it difficult to verify that the equations preserve attention mass as claimed.
Overall, the problem and high-level idea are promising, but the causal evidence, evaluation validity, baseline fairness, and reproducibility are not adequate for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and relatively underexplored failure mode: visual hallucinations can propagate and amplify through textual communication in VLM-based multi-agent systems.
ViF is intuitively motivated by the attention analyses and combines visual-token relay with attention reallocation in a conceptually coherent framework.

The empirical scope is impressive: eight benchmarks, four multi-agent structures, ten model configurations, multiple model families and sizes, comparisons with five hallucination-mitigation methods, and component and hyperparameter ablations.
The reported improvements are highly consistent across comprehensive and hallucination-focused benchmarks, with especially encouraging behavior as the number of agent turns increases.

The layer-wise token-dropping experiments, token visualizations, cross-model attention analyses, and Flash-Attention-compatible Key-Norm alternative provide useful supporting evidence beyond headline benchmark results.
weaknesses: The claimed causal explanation is substantially stronger than the evidence. Correlation between decreasing visual attention and hallucination does not establish that attention reduction causes snowballing, and attention magnitude is not necessarily a reliable measure of information use. Zeroing selected hidden states can also introduce distribution shift rather than cleanly measure token importance.

Crucial reproducibility details are missing: the exact agent prompts and roles, communication protocol, number of agents and turns used in each main table, definitions of shallow/middle/deep layer ranges, judge-model versions and prompts, training datasets and sample counts, and seed-level variability are not reported. The source-code URL is also blank in the submitted manuscript.

The method is described as lightweight and plug-and-play, but it introduces a trainable transformer block and uses two-stage pretraining and instruction tuning. No parameter count, training cost, inference latency, memory overhead, or token/communication overhead is reported, making the efficiency and deployment claims unsupported.

The custom HS metric is insufficiently validated and underspecified. The procedure for identifying individual hallucinations, assigning propagation distance and severity, and aggregating branching structures is unclear; the judge model is unspecified, and there is no human-agreement, robustness, or correlation analysis establishing that HS measures genuine propagation.

Important controls are absent. In particular, the paper does not compare against relaying an equal number of random, high-attention, or unmodified visual tokens; simply increasing visual-token capacity; re-encoding or re-supplying the image; or a token-budget-matched visual-memory baseline. Thus, the gains do not isolate the proposed unimodal-token selection mechanism.

Baseline comparisons against prior hallucination methods are restricted to one model and one MAS topology, while most large tables compare only the unmodified system with ViF. There is little comparison to methods specifically designed for multimodal agent communication or visual memory.

All results are single point estimates despite stochastic decoding with temperature 1. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests, so it is difficult to assess whether smaller gains—often around one benchmark point—are reliable.

The mathematical presentation of attention reallocation is ambiguous about row-wise attention normalization and causal masking, and the paper does not explain precisely how visual states produced by one model or agent are made compatible with another. This also limits the strength of the claimed applicability to arbitrary heterogeneous multi-agent systems.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored reliability problem: hallucinations can propagate and amplify during multi-agent visual reasoning.

ViF offers an intuitively appealing idea—preserving latent visual evidence between agents instead of communicating exclusively through generated text—and combines token selection with attention reallocation.
The empirical coverage is broad, spanning multiple VLM families and sizes, four communication structures, standard hallucination and general-purpose benchmarks, and multi-image/video settings.

The paper includes component ablations, turn-count analyses, efficiency measurements, hyperparameter studies, alternative token-selection mechanisms, adversarial-input experiments, and comparisons with several hallucination-mitigation methods.
The presentation is generally organized, and the reported improvements are consistent across the many configurations considered.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic conclusion is not established. Attention allocated to vision is summed by token type without adequate normalization for the number of tokens or context length. Because textual context grows across agent turns, declining visual attention mass may arise mechanically from increasing textual competition rather than explain hallucination propagation. Attention correlation and token-dropping interventions do not demonstrate that the disappearance of unimodal tokens causes snowballing.

The experimental comparison appears seriously confounded by training. ViF adds a trainable transformer and uses two-stage training in which even the LLM is trainable during instruction tuning, whereas the principal competitors are described as training-free methods applied to the base model. No training-matched control is provided, so the gains cannot be attributed specifically to visual relay or attention reallocation.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the large result tables. The manuscript does not specify the training datasets, objectives, number of agents used in the main experiments, topology sizes and sampled edges, complete prompts, benchmark sample counts, random seeds, or parameter/training cost. Temperature-1 generation is evaluated without uncertainty estimates or significance tests, making modest 1–3 point gains difficult to assess.

The claimed model-agnostic nature is overstated. The method requires access to internal visual representations, layer boundaries, keys or attention scores, architectural intervention, and model-specific training. All demonstrated systems use closely related open-weight VLM architectures, and heterogeneous agents with incompatible latent spaces are not evaluated.

It is unclear whether visual relay addresses a genuine communication constraint: downstream agents appear to receive the original visual tokens as well as relay tokens. If every agent already observes the original image, the method is better characterized as additional latent conditioning or visual memory than as transmission of otherwise unavailable evidence. Controls using an equally sized learned latent module or re-encoded original-image tokens are missing.

The proposed HS metric relies on a proprietary GPT-5 judge and an incompletely specified propagation distance. Validation only reports that 94% of Gemini discrepancies are below 10%, without human validation, agreement statistics, correlation, or judge-bias analysis. This is insufficient to support strong claims based on 30–40% HS reductions.

Several technical definitions are underspecified or inconsistent, including the exact unimodal-token criterion, middle/deep layer boundaries, dimensional interpretation and normalization of the reallocation equations, and how tokens are transferred while retaining positional information. The assertion that total attention remains one is not rigorously justified by the presented equations.

The ablations do not isolate important alternatives: a training-matched baseline, random-token relay with exactly matched count and training, relay without prior text, attention reallocation without added training, and controls for context length are needed. The current token-dropping experiments establish sensitivity to selected representations but not the claimed causal mechanism.

Some evaluation and reporting details contain inconsistencies, such as conflicting HallBench optimization directions and citation/benchmark-description errors. More importantly, there is no discussion of data contamination, benchmark reuse during instruction tuning, or ethical and deployment risks associated with multi-agent visual systems.

strengths: The paper identifies an important reliability problem: errors can propagate through textual communication in multi-agent vision-language systems.
ViF combines visual-token relay with attention reallocation in a conceptually intuitive framework, and the turn-wise performance analysis is relevant to the claimed failure mode.
The empirical study is broad in nominal coverage, spanning multiple VLM configurations, agent topologies, hallucination benchmarks, general multimodal benchmarks, and multi-image/video tasks.
The paper includes component ablations, efficiency measurements, hyperparameter sweeps, alternative token-selection mechanisms, and comparisons with several hallucination-mitigation methods.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established. Decreasing visual attention is correlated with later turns, but this does not show that it causes hallucination propagation. Token-dropping interventions are highly disruptive and do not constitute a controlled mediation analysis; attention weights themselves are also not reliable explanations of model behavior.

The attention analysis appears mathematically inconsistent and confounded. Equation 5 sums attention over all queries without clearly normalizing for the number of queries or tokens, despite reporting allocations on a 0–1 scale. Sequence composition and length change across turns, so raw category-level attention is not directly comparable unless token-count and query-count effects are controlled.

The attention-reallocation method is insufficiently defined. Equations 3–4 ambiguously mix attention scores, logits, and normalized weights, omit important indices, and do not clearly justify the claim that total attention remains one after reallocation and softmax. The definitions of layer ranges, inactive tokens, trend tolerance, and unimodal salience are also incomplete.

The experimental protocol for converting normally single-agent benchmarks into multi-agent tasks is not reproducible. Essential details such as agent prompts and roles, numbers of agents and rounds for each table, graph instantiation, image access at each node, message construction, stopping rules, and final-answer selection are missing. These choices could materially determine whether snowballing occurs.

ViF is not evaluated against the most important simple and controlled alternatives, such as re-feeding the original image or its complete visual embeddings at every turn, sharing a fixed visual memory, using matched randomly selected tokens, or training an equal-capacity communication module. Most reported competitors are single-agent decoding methods and therefore do not isolate the benefit of the proposed inter-agent communication design.

The training description is seriously incomplete. The paper introduces a trainable transformer block and claims two-stage pretraining and instruction tuning, but provides no training datasets, data volumes, objectives, sampling procedure, initialization, or per-model training details. Consequently, it is impossible to determine whether improvements arise from ViF or additional multimodal training, and the work cannot be reproduced. The promised source-code link is also empty in the manuscript.

Reported gains lack uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests despite generation temperature 1 and many gains being only about 0.5–3 points. The unusually uniform improvements across many model–topology–benchmark combinations need stronger statistical support and independent validation.

The proposed HS score does not convincingly measure propagation. Its hallucination distance is not operationally defined for the different graph structures, and a distance-weighted sum of independently judged hallucination severities cannot distinguish propagation of an earlier error from unrelated later errors. Agreement between two proprietary judges on only POPE, reported merely as the fraction differing by less than 10%, does not validate the metric.

The claim of being model-agnostic is overstated: the method requires internal visual tokens, layer-specific interventions, attention modification, model-dependent hooks, and additional training. The Key-Norm approximation helps with inaccessible attention matrices but does not remove these architectural requirements.

Novelty and positioning are weaker than presented. Prior work already studies multimodal hallucination snowballing, visual-memory/token relay, and attention-based visual steering; the paper does not sharply establish which technical element is fundamentally new beyond combining these ingredients in a multi-agent setup. Overall, the breadth of tables does not compensate for the unresolved soundness, control, and reproducibility issues.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored failure mode in vision-language multi-agent systems: erroneous visual information can propagate and become amplified through text-only inter-agent communication.

ViF is intuitively motivated and combines visual-token relaying with attention reallocation. The reported improvements are highly consistent across four MAS topologies, ten VLM backbones of several sizes, and a broad collection of image, multi-image, video, general-purpose, and hallucination benchmarks.

The evaluation includes several useful analyses beyond headline accuracy: comparisons with five hallucination-mitigation methods, component ablations, turn-count scaling, adversarial visual inputs, hyperparameter sensitivity, and latency/FLOP measurements.

The experiments suggest that ViF becomes especially helpful with longer interactions and denser communication, matching the motivating hypothesis. The computational overhead is moderate and decreases proportionally for larger models.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and its attention and token visualizations make the proposed phenomenon and method accessible.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is insufficiently established. The paper primarily shows correlation between reduced visual attention and increased hallucination, then treats attention allocation as a causal explanation. Attention weights are not necessarily faithful importance measures, and the token-dropping intervention introduces substantial out-of-distribution activation changes. Controlled interventions separating context length, accumulated textual content, and actual error propagation are needed.

Reproducibility is a major concern. ViF requires a two-stage training pipeline, but the training datasets, sampling procedure, objectives and losses, initialization, checkpoint selection, and per-backbone training details are not specified. The promised source-code link is empty in the manuscript.

Several technical definitions are unclear or potentially inconsistent. The attention-allocation equation sums attention over all query tokens yet is discussed as a normalized allocation; the collection/reallocation equations have ambiguous dimensions and normalization; shallow, middle, and deep layer boundaries are not stated; and the precise algorithm for detecting unimodal tokens is underspecified beyond a threshold.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests despite stochastic generation with temperature 1. Many reported gains are modest, so it is difficult to determine their robustness. Hyperparameters also appear to be selected on the same benchmark/model configuration used for reporting, with no validation protocol described.

The proposed HS metric is not independently validated. Its propagation distance is insufficiently defined, it relies on a proprietary judge, and agreement with Gemini is reported only as the fraction of discrepancies below 10% on POPE. This does not establish correlation with human judgments or show that HS measures propagation rather than ordinary per-turn hallucination.

The claimed model-agnosticism is overstated: the method requires access to internal vision tokens, keys or attention scores, layer-wise interventions, and backbone-specific retraining. It therefore does not apply directly to API-only or architecturally opaque VLM agents.

The baselines are mainly single-agent hallucination mitigators transplanted into the authors' MAS framework. The study would be more convincing with stronger multi-agent communication baselines, such as passing selected image regions/features, repeated image access, learned multimodal memory, or matched token-budget controls. A complete ablation removing all relay tokens and direct controls for extra visual tokens/training capacity are also missing.
